items.title: If implemented to the letter, 24-Hour Economy will be a game changer – AGI
items.description: The Association of Ghana Industries (AGI) has welcomed government’s 24-Hour Economy policy, saying its successful implementation could significantly transform Ghana’s industrial sector. AGI President Seth Twum Akwaboah, speaking on Joy News’ PM Express Business Edition on Thursday, said the business community was more interested in the policy’s substance than in the slogan attached to it. “For me, I don’t bother so much about the clichés you create, whether it’s 24-Hour Economy or 1D1F; that’s not really the issue for me. It is more of what you do within those policies,” he said. According to him, the effectiveness of the policy will depend largely on how it is designed and implemented, particularly the extent to which industry players are consulted. “You can come up with any policy, but then, when you develop the policy, what has gone into the policy development? How consultative was its nature? What are the key policies or activities within the policy that you are trying to implement to change the status quo?” he asked. Mr Twum Akwaboah said the 24-Hour Economy concept was initially unclear to businesses, but engagements with government have helped provide greater clarity on its intended direction. He cautioned against expectations that the policy would immediately transform economic activity across the country. “When you hear a cliché, when you hear a mention of something like that, sometimes the expectation is that overnight things will change and everything will be a 24-hour economy. It doesn’t happen like that,” he said. He drew a parallel with the One District, One Factory (1D1F) initiative, saying its announcement did not mean every district would immediately have an industrial facility. “The same thing I said is that when we had the 1D1F. All of a sudden, you think that every district is going to have an industry? Government has mentioned it. It’s an intention. It’s a vision. How do we work towards it?” he said. He said the same principle should guide the 24-Hour Economy, with government identifying specific activities, policies and programmes required to achieve its objectives. “The same thing applies to the 24-hour economy. So I’m not expecting that things will change overnight like that. But then we need to define the specific activities and policies and programs we are going to do to make that happen,” he said. Mr Twum Akwaboah noted that government had made progress by launching a blueprint for the policy, which he said contains several ideas that could benefit the economy if properly executed. “And gradually they are coming to that point where now they’ve launched a blueprint, and then in it there are a lot of interesting ideas. If we’re able to implement it to the letter, I’m sure it will help change a lot of things,” he said. He reaffirmed the AGI’s support for the initiative and disclosed that the association is working with government and the 24-Hour Economy Secretariat on aspects of the policy. “So for me, I embrace it just as we embraced the 1D1F, AGI embraces the 24-hour economy, and we are working with government. “We are working with the 24-hour economy secretariat to implement some of the things they said they will implement,” he said. Mr Twum Akwaboah believes the policy could ultimately have a major impact on Ghana’s economy if government follows through on its commitments. “If we’re able to do it, it will be a game changer,” he said.

items.title: Two-Nation Theory and genesis of Pakistan
items.description: IN South Asia, the rise of Muslim political consciousness and the creation of Pakistan reflected a prolonged constitutional and political struggle led by Quaid-i-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah. The demand for Pakistan was rooted in the belief that the Muslims of British India constituted a distinct political community whose cultural, religious, and political interests required constitutional protection and effective political representation. Pakistan’s national identity has consequently remained closely associated with the ideas that formed the raison d’être for the Pakistan Movement. Its history offers lessons that can be learnt from significant events, most notably the political crisis of 1971, which culminated in the separation of East Pakistan. The post-1971 period also witnessed continuing debates over the nature of the federation, provincial autonomy, and national identity. These debates underline the importance of learning from history rather than using it to promote narrow political narratives. Pakistan’s political experience demonstrates that national cohesion depends not only on shared historical ideals but also on constitutional governance, political inclusion, social justice, and respect for diversity. The enduring challenge, therefore, is to reconcile Pakistan’s historical foundations with the requirements of a modern, democratic, and inclusive state to dispel the spread of unsubstantiated narratives against the Two-Nation Theory as an ideological basis of Pakistan. Pakistan’s leadership must follow the Quaid’s democratic vision and understand the primacy of Jinnah’s thoughts in tackling constitutional, political, economic and security challenges. The dilemma that crystallised after the 1857 War of Independence was the result of wilful distortions and misconceptions about the Muslims of British India. The British believed that Muslims were the real ‘troublemakers’ responsible for the uprising. Their hostile attitude towards Muslims caused exploitation and generated feelings of deprivation among them. They lost social status and suffered cruel punishments. During this dark phase of the community’s life Sir Syed Ahmad Khan dispelled the idea that Muslims were responsible for the war. The Aligarh movement he launched was based on a trinity of ideas: loyalty to the British, distance from politics, and devotion to education. His educational movement started to bring lasting change in the outlook of Muslim community. In the beginning Sir Syed was in favour of Hindu-Muslim unity; he considered India as a bride and Hindus and Muslims as the two eyes of the bride. Nevertheless, in 1867, after the Hindi-Urdu controversy, he realised that both communities were separate. Thus, Muslims became aware of their own distinctive political identity in the subcontinent. They acted on the advice of Sir Syed and cooperated with the British. They did not join the Indian National Congress (INC), which was established in 1885 to provide a common platform for Indians and to introduce the concept of one nation. It was clear that the organisation based on Western type of democracy would not be able to protect Muslim interests due to dominance of Hindus. Crystallisation of Sir Syed’s thoughts formed the Two-Nation Theory. It was not only the religious and social aspect of life where there were divergences between the two communities. There were little or no common customs and traditions shared by both communities. The structure, function and shape of houses and places of worship belonging to both communities were different. The variance was much wider in cuisine. There were no common festivals and celebrations among Hindus and Muslims. The language spoken by Hindus and Muslims was Hindustani, used for the purpose of communication. However, for literary purposes Muslims used Urdu, which absorbed many Arabic, Persian and Turkish words. Hindus used Hindi as a source of literature, which consisted of high percentage of Sanskrit words. Thus, both languages expressed fundamentally different ideas and shared different cultural expressions. This difference went deeper in poetry. Urdu poetry expressed themes of loneliness, amazement, and depiction of Muslim life shared across many countries in a very different way using metaphors, abstraction, and philosophical manner compared to Hindi poetry, which depicted local environment and described emotions. Muslims realised that they had different outlook, beliefs, traditions, language, and inclinations. Their apprehension of losing their status and suppression of their identity motivated them to bring homogeneity to their nationhood under the prevailing claustrophobic social and political order. The Two-Nation Theory impelled its adherents to follow a joint line of action for the accomplishment of their goal. It shaped the ideological form of the Pakistan Movement and gave birth to a new nation. The Two-Nation Theory was a revolt against the prevailing exploitation of Muslims by the British and domination of Hindus in British India, where Hinduism was being imposed on Muslims and their culture. Based on the Two-Nation Theory Muslims demanded a separate electorate in 1906. The British, through the Minto-Morley reforms, allowed separate electorates by recognising Muslims as a separate nation. Achieving separate statutory status was a triumph and proved a hallmark in Indian politics. Through the Lucknow Pact of 1916, the Quaid tried to bring the two communities closer, and he was called the “ambassador of Hindu-Muslim unity”. It was a tremendous achievement of Jinnah that Congress also recognised Muslims as a separate nation. Jinnah worked towards the goal of uniting both communities until M.K. Gandhi started playing the communal card. Gandhi publicly said that “a body of converts cannot call themselves a nation.” In response to this the Quaid replied in a public statement that by all canons of international law, the Muslims constituted a nation. Quaid-i-Azam understood that the Indian Muslims could compete with the Congress only when they showed they could settle their own differences. Jinnah declared the Muslims to be a nation with its own “distinctive culture and civilisation, language and literature, art and architecture, names and nomenclature, sense of values and proportion, legal laws and moral codes, customs and calendar, history and tradition, aptitude and ambition.” The expression of the Two-Nation Theory was reflected in his famous 14 Points. This legal framework provided for effective representation of Muslims in all law-making bodies, protection of Muslim territories, their religious liberty, culture, language, education, personal laws, customs, and their religious institutions. The movement for the partition of India gained strength when the poet-philosopher Allama Dr Muhammad Iqbal conceived the geographical shape of a homeland for Muslims. During his address in 1930 at Allahabad, Allama Iqbal said: “I would like to see the Punjab, North-West Frontier Province, Sindh and Baluchistan amalgamated into a single state. Self-government within the British Empire, or the formation of a consolidated North-West Indian Muslim state, appears to me to be the final destiny of the Muslims at least of North-West India.” The Quaid’s return from England to India in 1934 marked a turning point in politics. He was convinced that constitutional safeguards alone might not secure the political future of India’s Muslims, and began to articulate a more determined vision of separate homeland for Muslims by converting Iqbal’s dream into reality. The Government of India Act 1935 introduced provincial autonomy, expanded the electorate, and established provincial legislatures. Despite reservations, both the Congress and the Muslim League contested the 1937 elections. Congress emerged victorious in several provinces and formed ministries, including in areas with Muslim majority. The Congress rule proved politically devastating for Muslims. The Congress ministries promoted Hindu culture and policies at the expense of Muslim identity. The Wardha education scheme became a particular source of controversy. Congress, for revival of Hinduism, introduced Wardha scheme to downgrade Muslims, exploit their resources and impose Hindu values, customs, and traditions. The Pirpur Report of 1938, prepared by a committee headed by Raja Muhammad Mehdi, documented alleged discrimination against Muslims, while A.K. Fazlul Huq’s Muslim Suffering Under Congress Rule presented further claims of Muslim grievances. Jinnah turned these grievances into a wider political argument. Addressing the Sindh Provincial Muslim League Conference in Karachi in 1938, he criticised the Congress leadership for its hostile attitude towards the Muslim League. At the League’s Patna session later that year, he argued that Congress rule had further weakened the prospects of a genuine Hindu-Muslim settlement. The resignation of Congress ministries in 1939, following the outbreak of the Second World War, gave Jinnah another opportunity to consolidate Muslim political opinion. He called December 22 the ‘Day of Deliverance’, presenting the end of Congress rule as a moment of political relief for Muslims. Yet the significance of 1937-39 extended beyond immediate grievances. The experience convinced many Muslims that a political system dominated by a permanent majority could threaten their cultural, economic, and political interests. Jinnah responded by reorganising the Muslim League, strengthening its finances and parliamentary machinery, and transforming it from an elite organisation into a mass political movement. The Congress rule thus became an important catalyst in the development of Muslim political consciousness. Under Jinnah’s leadership, the League increasingly transformed Muslim apprehensions into a coherent political demand, ultimately paving the way for the Pakistan Movement. The Lahore Resolution was adopted by the All-India Muslim League at Lahore in its 27th annual session on March 23, 1940. Congress leaders, including Jawaharlal Nehru and Gandhi, opposed the Lahore Resolution, which they termed the “Pakistan Resolution”, arguing that it threatened the idea of a united India. Two years later, in 1942, British minister Sir Stafford Cripps arrived in India to resolve the political deadlock and secure Indian cooperation in the Second World War. His proposals offered India dominion status after the war and the right to frame its own constitution. The Provinces were given the option of not joining the proposed Indian Union, while the princely states were offered participation in the constitutional arrangement. Congress rejected the proposals because it wanted an immediate transfer of power, rather than waiting until after the war. The Muslim League also rejected them, as the scheme did not explicitly recognise its demand for a separate Muslim state. By then, the League was firmly committed to the political direction set by the Lahore Resolution. With the end of WWII in 1945, the British government faced mounting pressure to resolve India’s constitutional crisis. Viceroy Lord Wavell invited the Congress and Muslim League leadership to the Simla Conference, proposing greater transfer of power to Indians while retaining the viceroy as a constitutional head. The conference, however, failed to bridge the differences between Congress and the Muslim League, particularly over Muslim representation. The British subsequently turned to elections to gauge political support. In the 1945-46 elections, the Muslim League achieved a remarkable victory, winning all 30 Muslim-reserved seats in the Central Legislative Assembly and about 95 per cent of the Muslim seats in the provincial legislatures. The results strengthened Jinnah’s claim that the League represented the political aspirations of India’s Muslims and provided a powerful electoral mandate for the demand for a separate homeland. In February 1946, the British government sent the Cabinet Mission, comprising Lord Pethick-Lawrence, Sir Stafford Cripps and A.V. Alexander, to negotiate a constitutional settlement. Its plan proposed a relatively weak central government responsible mainly for defence, foreign affairs and communications, while provinces retained substantial autonomy. Although the plan did not fully satisfy the Muslim League’s demand for Pakistan, Jinnah initially saw the reflection of the Two-Nation Theory within its proposed system of provincial groupings. The political crisis deepened when disagreements emerged over the interpretation and implementation of the plan, particularly the grouping of provinces and the formation of an interim government. The Muslim League eventually withdrew its acceptance and called for direct action to press its demand. Jinnah announced Aug 16, 1946 as Direct Action Day. By the end of 1946, the debate over provincial grouping had further sharpened the political divide and Jinnah’s point of view gained immense prominence and increased the momentum for creation of a new country. Since our independence, Pakistan’s record of experimenting with almost every form of government indicates that the successive rulers have failed to understand the Quaid’s vision for statehood. Our history as a nation is replete with political crises that perhaps no other country in the world has experienced because we deviated from Jinnah’s principles, ideals, and vision. Thus, crime and corruption are rapidly becoming a way of life. Aversion to the rule of law, poor governance and economic downfall have become formidable challenges due to inchoate nature of institutions. The political institutions have failed to deliver, and people’s aspirations have not been fulfilled. As a result, people began to shift their loyalties and looked towards alternative religious and ethnic-based platforms which paved the way for undemocratic forces and planted the seeds of extremism, radicalisation, ethnic nationalism, and sectarian violence. These challenges were not properly dealt with by the leadership in the nascent state of Pakistan and thus the feelings of ethnic nationalism permeated both East Pakistan and West Pakistan, which triggered disunity and disintegration. The purpose of the Two-Nation Theory was to create a separate homeland for Muslims. The battle between the Muslim League and Congress was political, not religious. In a 1948 speech the Quaid said: Islam and its idealism have taught democracy, equality, and fair play. After the creation of Pakistan, few world leaders could anticipate that it would be able to survive under the difficult circumstances created by India. On the other hand, it was expected that the Quaid would provide strong leadership, which was badly needed, when he assumed the office of governor-general. He stood like a mighty oak in a storm following independence. His strength was essential for the infant country and no greater fortune could have come to the new country than Jinnah’s acceptance of being its first head of state. Nevertheless, due to the inability of his successors to overcome their disagreements, jealousies, and personal rivalries, it took almost a decade to form the country’s first constitution in 1956, which was abrogated under martial law, imposed in 1958. General Ayub Khan gave a presidential constitution in 1962 and another martial law was imposed in 1969. Later, elections were held in 1970. However, Pakistan faced the tragic separation of East Pakistan. Eventually, after a huge lapse of time, a truly remarkable document — the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan 1973 — was finalised, which has been the basis of Pakistan’s government. The country remained under martial law from 1977 to 1985, with most provisions of the 1973 Constitution held in abeyance. The Ziaul Haq regime (1977-1988) patronised religionisation of politics, created polarisation among various classes in society, encouraged sectarian divide and nurtured extremism. Another authoritarian era — that of Pervez Musharraf (1999-2008) — offered numerous lessons for civilian and military ruling elites. However, the track record of political elites belonging to major political parties in the later decades of democracy indicates that they have not demonstrated a commitment to the rule of law and showed inability to respect the Constitution. Ruling elites remained entrenched in power in violation of the principles and spirit of the Constitution. Thus, the supremacy of the Constitution was compromised. The lack of continuous dialogue among democratic forces to discuss economic and governance issues has caused disillusionment among the masses with the democratic system, which is exposed to vulnerable situation of terrorist insurgencies, socio-economic disparities, and volatile nature of geopolitics under changing dynamics of international politics. These challenges deserve attention of competent, honest, and efficient leadership to deal with the monumental issues confronting Pakistan today, including a fractured political system and economic chaos. Pakistan’s leadership must follow the Quaid’s democratic vision and understand the primacy of Jinnah’s thoughts in tackling constitutional, political, economic and security challenges faced by Pakistan and to come up with a new solution to perennial problems. Our leaders need to promote integration and unity in the country through societal transformation, which requires firm belief in democratic norms and values including liberty, equality, justice, and fair play. There is no reason for anybody to fear democracy, equality of all citizens, inclusivity and cultural diversity. All we need is to be united and make Pakistan a strong nation which should lead the Muslim world towards a peaceful future. The writer is an academic.

items.description: Este sábado aparece marcado en rojo en el calendario de los responsables del Ministerio del Interior, pero también en el de las autoridades marroquíes. En las redes sociales circulan desde hace días mensajes que alientan a repetir las escenas vividas los pasados 30 y 31 de julio con miles de migrantes entrando de manera irregular en Ceuta a nado, bordeando el espigón de El Tarajal. “La frontera de Ceuta estará abierta el día 15 [de agosto], festivo en España”, rezan algunos mensajes difundidos a través de internet para animar a participar en una nueva irrupción masiva. Ante ello, Rabat ha reforzado el puesto fronterizo de Fnideq (Castillejos en su denominación colonial española) con cientos de miembros de las fuerzas de seguridad apoyados por tropas militares, según se observa en vídeos que circulan desde hace casi una semana en medios digitales del país magrebí. También se han difundido imágenes de la instalación de concertinas y alambradas en las vallas que marcan el límite fronterizo del lado marroquí. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Las palabras de Albares activan el temor a la devolución entre los migrantes llegados a nado a Ceuta
items.description: “Ya han llegado a un acuerdo”, escribe Siraj en su teléfono. Tiene 16 años y lleva casi dos semanas en Ceuta, desde que el 30 de julio cruzó a nado desde Marruecos. El mensaje va dirigido a un amigo que, como él, permanece en la ciudad autónoma. Le cuenta lo que acaba de escuchar: el ministro de Asuntos Exteriores , José Manuel Albares, ha hablado en conferencia de prensa. No ha pasado ni media hora desde su intervención, pero el mensaje ya corre de móvil en móvil. En los grupos de WhatsApp y las redes sociales de los jóvenes que llegaron a nado, la noticia se propaga como un reguero de pólvora. Para muchos, esas palabras confirman el peor de sus temores. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Antonio Maíllo: “Marruecos ha cometido una acción criminal con muertes. Hay que replantearse todo”
items.description: Antonio Maíllo (Lucena, Córdoba, 59 años) está estos días en la sierra de Huelva, donde sigue pendiente de los incendios que asolan a la provincia con más de 25.000 hectáreas calcinadas. El coordinador general de Izquierda Unida atiende a EL PAÍS por teléfono y defiende un cambio radical en las relaciones diplomáticas con Marruecos, a quien tacha de cometer una “acción criminal” que ha provocado muertes en Ceuta. Seguir leyendo

items.title: ¿Por qué se ha encarecido más el diésel que la gasolina?
items.description: Los precios de los combustibles continúan su escalada, con el diésel a la cabeza. Este carburante ha superado los 1,82 euros por litro, encadenando así un mes y medio de alzas consecutivas, mientras que la gasolina ha traspasado el umbral de los 1,70 euros, según los últimos datos del boletín petrolero de la Unión Europea. El encarecimento del gasóleo ha provocado que se vaya a activar en septiembre la cláusula de salvaguarda del escudo anticrisis para elevar la rebaja fiscal de este carburante hasta los 20 céntimos por litro, frente a los 5 céntimos inicialmente previstos. La medida se pone en marcha porque el precio del diésel se ha encarecido más de un 15% en términos interanuales, mientras que la gasolina seguirá el calendario establecido porque su coste aumentó interanualmente un 7,3%. Los expertos consultados atribuyen esta diferencia en la evolución de precios a la mayor demanda de diésel en España, pero sobre todo a las tensiones en los mercados energéticos provocadas por las guerras en Ucrania e Irán. Seguir leyendo

items.title: La casa del portero es ya un negocio inmobiliario en Madrid: “Reformada, genera unos 1.000 euros al mes para los vecinos”
items.description: Bastan 20 segundos de búsqueda en algún portal inmobiliario para comprobar que en Madrid hasta la casa del portero se ha convertido en un negocio inmobiliario. Y es cada vez más lucrativo. En un edificio de la calle del Doctor Castelo, en Retiro, un anuncio destaca que “la antigua vivienda del portero ha sido reformada y actualmente genera unos ingresos aproximados de 1.000 euros mensuales para la comunidad”. En otro inmueble de Ciudad Jardín, el comprador se lleva, junto con el piso, “el 3,32% de la antigua casa del portero”: un ático que la comunidad está reformando para alquilar. Seguir leyendo

items.title: La matriarca de las orcas ‘gladis’, de 60 años, aparece con impactos de perdigones en la aleta
items.description: El 10 de agosto un equipo de científicos avistó a Toñi , la matriarca de más edad de la población de orcas ibéricas y guardiana de una sabiduría de décadas que transmite a su grupo, nadando con dos compañeras por el Estrecho de Gibraltar. Hacía dos años que no se la veía por allí. Fue en ese momento cuando detectaron que presentaba unas marcas en la aleta dorsal compatibles con disparos de una escopeta de perdigones. Una vez analizados, no les queda ninguna duda de que recibió 10 impactos y que algunos continúan alojados en su aleta, por lo que existe el riesgo de que se pueda producir una infección. Toñi , también conocida como La Abuela , no es cualquier orca: tiene 60 años y es, además, la bisabuela, abuela y madre de las conocidas como gladis , los ejemplares que protagonizan desde mayo de 2022 polémicos encuentros con embarcaciones. Seguir leyendo

items.title: ¿Para qué sirve un ‘concierge’, un restaurador o un ‘coach’ de nutrición en un hotel?
items.description: Los hoteles quieren dejar huella en sus huéspedes para hacerlos volver. Por eso personalizan sus servicios al extremo en una carrera por ofrecer experiencias tan privadas que apenas puedan replicarse con otros clientes. Para conseguirlo, escuchan historias personales, deseos por cumplir, viajes por hacer realidad. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Nina Lykke: “Los hijos en Noruega están al mando de una forma descabellada. La autoridad está muy denostada”
items.description: Nina Lykke (Trondheim, 61 años) empezó a publicar sus novelas cuando ya mediaba la cuarentena. Creció en la capital noruega, tuvo dos hijas y un trabajo como maquetadora y diseñadora gráfica freelance . Toda una vida al margen de los premios y el reconocimiento de los lectores que más tarde ha alcanzado esta autora, una de las voces más destacadas y caústicas de la literatura nórdica actual. Seguir leyendo ¿Dónde están los adultos? Nina Lykke Traducción de Ana Flecha Marco Gatopardo, 2026 216 páginas. 19,95 euros

items.title: Ventajas de tener un megáfono en la mesilla
items.description: No sé cuántos años hace. Nunca recuerdo cuándo sucedieron las cosas. Mi aversión por los números —esas letras raras— se extiende a fechas, números de pisos, casas y sucesos históricos. Lo único que permanece imborrable son las cantidades monetarias. Aquel verano cobré 500 euros por ser camarera en un chiringuito durante las fiestas del Orgullo en Chueca. ¡Y me parecía mucho dinero! (Preveo bastantes exclamaciones escandalizadas en este texto). Seguir leyendo

items.title: Ceuta, de los tacticismos banales a la mirada estratégica
items.description: Hay crisis que ponen a prueba a quien gobierna. Otras, por su envergadura, al país entero. Unas pocas de ellas, a toda Europa. La de Ceuta pertenece a esa triple categoría combinada. Hace dos semanas, más de 70.000 marroquíes arriesgaron la vida —más de un centenar de ellos la perdió, sin que conste consternación de sus autoridades— y estuvieron en juego la estabilidad de la ciudad, la credibilidad internacional de España y la seguridad exterior de la UE. Seguir leyendo

items.title: El ‘momento Aranzadi’ de Vox
items.description: Vox atraviesa su momento Aranzadi . Desde hace tiempo, existe un recelo sutil en la ultraderecha sobre si a Alberto Núñez Feijóo le temblarán las piernas a la hora de derogar muchas leyes de la izquierda, en el caso de llegar a La Moncloa. Hay quien incluso teme que el Partido Popular y Vox se arrojen a una eventual legislatura en balde. Santiago Abascal lo fía ahora todo a demostrar que sí se puede controlar el BOE, y a Feijóo debería preocuparle el giro institucionalista de sus socios. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Hacienda limita la rebaja fiscal al vender el piso de soltero para comprar una casa en pareja
items.description: Debate cerrado. Quien venda su casa de soltero para comprar o construir una nueva junto a su cónyuge no siempre podrá aplicar la exención en el IRPF por reinversión en vivienda habitual sobre la totalidad de la ganancia que ha obtenido. Solo se le permitirá acogerse al incentivo por el importe correspondiente a la parte del nuevo hogar que realmente le pertenezca —habitualmente, la mitad—, independientemente de cuánto dinero destine a su adquisición. Así lo ha establecido el Tribunal Económico Administrativo Central (TEAC) en una reciente resolución que unifica criterios y obliga a la Agencia Tributaria a seguir esta interpretación: lo que cuenta es la propiedad, y no quién ponga el dinero. Seguir leyendo

items.title: La “carrera de obstáculos” de las afganas para pedir el traslado a España: años de espera, documentos “imposibles” y recursos judiciales
items.description: Zahra no era una activista cuando los talibanes tomaron el poder en Afganistán el 15 de agosto de 2021 , hace cinco años. Sin embargo, esta joven, cuya identidad se oculta con un nombre falso, entonces de 22 años, salió a la calle a manifestarse cuando esos fundamentalistas empezaron a arrebatar a las afganas sus derechos: primero el de la educación; poco después, el del trabajo. Según su relato, en una de las protestas, el 4 de septiembre de 2021, agentes de la inteligencia de los talibanes le pusieron una bolsa negra en la cabeza, la metieron en un coche, se la llevaron a un centro de detención y la tuvieron allí secuestrada tres días. “Le hicieron de todo”, resume contrita las torturas María López, jurista de Netwomening, una asociación de asistencia a las afganas con protección internacional en España. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Alessia Schiavon, jurista: “Afganistán parece un cuento distópico. Están borrando a las mujeres de la sociedad”
items.description: Hay personas que trabajan con objetivos a corto plazo, como un cirujano al salvar una vida en el quirófano. Otras lo hacen con la mirada puesta en un horizonte que saben lejano, pero sin por ello detenerse, como quienes trabajan para mejorar la protección de los seres humanos a través de herramientas jurídicas cuya aplicación efectiva puede llevar años. Es el caso de RAGAA , una iniciativa de la Fundación Internacional Baltasar Garzón (Fibgar) y de la asociación People Help (PH), que buscan impulsar el reconocimiento del apartheid de género como crimen internacional. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Ahmed y Saleh, niños amputados de Gaza, aprenden a nadar: “El agua es el único lugar en el que son libres”
items.description: Ahmed al Masri cierra los ojos, se deja caer hacia atrás y flota. Un monitor permanece a su lado en una pequeña piscina que les cubre hasta la cintura y poco a poco lo suelta. Es la segunda clase de natación para este adolescente palestino de 14 años, que perdió su pierna derecha en julio de 2025 cuando salió a buscar comida para su familia en un momento en que el hambre golpeaba Gaza con tanta fuerza como los bombardeos israelíes. Seguir leyendo

items.title: La guerra del grano vuelve al mar Negro: Rusia bloquea las exportaciones de Ucrania y amenaza la próxima cosecha
items.description: La guerra de Ucrania vuelve a librarse sobre una de las arterias más sensibles de la economía mundial: el comercio de cereales . Los ataques rusos contra los puertos y buques ucranios en el mar Negro han reducido en las últimas semanas las exportaciones de grano a mínimos, justo cuando el país afronta el pico de la cosecha de trigo y se prepara para comenzar la recogida de maíz. Seguir leyendo

items.title: La millonaria lavadora de fondos de los narcos del puerto de Valencia: ladrillo, ‘criptos’ y gimnasios
items.description: El caudal de fondos de la coca que penetra en el puerto de Valencia se lava a través de un esquema mercantil de ladrillo, compañías de transporte, clínicas de entrenamiento y nutrición y criptomonedas. Bajo esta tesis, el magistrado del juzgado de Instrucción número 15 de Valencia, Vicente Ríos, que indaga a una red que almacenaba 4,5 toneladas de esta droga (60 millones de euros en el mercado), rastrea una opaca madeja empresarial para mover el dinero del polvo blanco, según los documentos a los que ha tenido acceso EL PAÍS. El esquema bajo sospecha incluye a familiares de los narcos —padres, esposas, primos— y se ideó para centrifugar las ganancias de esta multinacional del crimen desmantelada en 2025 en la Operación Spider . El mecanismo incluye singulares manejos, como narcos que transfieren su fortuna a su esposa en un falso divorcio para evitar que el patrimonio caiga en las garras de la justicia. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Etienne Krug, directivo de la OMS: “Los accidentes de tráfico son la primera causa de muerte entre los jóvenes”
items.description: El médico Etienne Krug (Amberes, Bélgica; 64 años) utiliza todos los días la bicicleta eléctrica para dirigirse desde su vivienda en la frontera de Francia con Suiza y desplazarse hasta la sede de la Organización Mundial de la Salud (OMS) en Ginebra. Son 20 kilómetros que realiza en un camino rodeado de viñedos. En la oficina, dirige el Departamento de Determinantes Sociales de la Salud de la OMS, un organismo en el que trabaja desde hace 28 años. Entre sus cometidos está la seguridad vial y el millón de personas que pierden la vida en el mundo al año. Recientemente ha estado en Madrid para participar en la XII Asamblea General del Observatorio Iberoamericano de Seguridad Vial (Oisevi). Seguir leyendo

items.title: Así son las vacaciones más saludables, según la ciencia: mejor largas y con actividad deportiva de por medio
items.description: Dos o tres meses de vacaciones son necesarios. Lo dijo un presidente de Estados Unidos, William Taft, en 1910: “Después del duro y agotador trabajo al que uno se somete entre el otoño y la primavera, [esos meses de descanso] son necesarios para poder continuar el trabajo al año siguiente con la energía y la eficacia que se merece”. Sus declaraciones propiciaron entonces un debate en The New York Times sobre cuánto deberían durar las vacaciones. Y, aunque un siglo después, la polémica no está resuelta, la ciencia ha ido afinando cómo tienen que ser esos parones veraniegos para descansar y recuperarse bien. Según los expertos consultados, con vacaciones largas se adquiere más bienestar, y también se maximizan los beneficios del descanso si se incorpora actividad deportiva por el medio. Es importante también establecer buenas rutinas de sueño y alimentación, y que exista una desconexión psicológica real del trabajo para que el parón sea verdaderamente reparador. Seguir leyendo

items.title: La Aemet avisa de un cambio de tiempo “importante” el fin de semana: tormentas fuertes tras el calor
items.description: Este fin de semana se va a producir un cambio de tiempo “brusco e importante”, ha alertado la Agencia Estatal de Meteorología (Aemet) en una nota informativa . Por un lado, y esto es una excelente noticia, el calor será menos intenso en buena parte de España, aunque todavía en la mitad sur y en Mallorca se superarán de 36° a 38°, incluso de los 38° en puntos del Guadalquivir. Pero lo destacable es “el incremento de la inestabilidad”: se esperan “chubascos y tormentas intensos en amplias zonas del interior peninsular”, que también podrán llegar a Baleares y que localmente podrán ser persistentes y fuertes y causar destrozos, como lo sucedido la tarde del jueves en Huelma (Jaén). Seguir leyendo

items.title: Halle Berry cumple 60 años: cinco motivos por los que se ha erigido en un icono de Hollywood
items.description: Halle Berry es, ante todo, lista. Como mujer que lleva casi cuatro décadas en la industria cinematográfica , la de Ohio es plenamente consciente de que a partir de cierta edad es prácticamente imposible que en las entrevistas no afloren cuestiones sobre el envejecimiento, la madurez, las nuevas etapas de la vida. La actriz cumple 60 años este viernes 14 de agosto y, sabedora de que este redondo aniversario iba a darle visibilidad, ha aprovechado para rentabilizar la mediática ocasión con el lanzamiento de un gel hidratante vaginal para mujeres menopáusicas. Juicy like a peach es el resultado de la asociación de la intérprete con la marca de bienestar íntimo Joylux, y su promoción es la excusa perfecta para preguntarle cómo se siente ante el cambio de década. “Me siento muy bien al respecto. Siento que estoy en el mejor momento de mi vida, como actriz y en todo lo que hago. He llamado a este periodo ‘mi mejor momento’ y realmente lo creo”, aseguró en una entrevista reciente para Hello! Seguir leyendo

items.title: “Mirad sus brazos. Está buenísimo”: el auge de los políticos guapos se hace viral
items.description: “Los peinados, la ropa, el calzado que usa la gente y el aspecto exterior” constituyen las leyes no escritas sobre las que se funda un Estado, escribió Platón en su República, demostrando así que ya entonces el físico de los políticos desempeñaba un papel fundamental en su poder e influencia. En el ensayo Lincoln’s Body , Richard Fox indagaba en la manera en que el físico de Abraham Lincoln -a quien, según comenta el autor, la prensa tachaba habitualmente de feo- marcó su carrera y su legado político. “Ya casi no hay gente fea presentándose a las elecciones”, apostilló. Seguir leyendo

items.title: El narco devora el aguacate mexicano
items.description: El comercio de aguacate entre México y Estados Unidos es un espejo de esa combinación de dependencia mutua y tensiones que caracteriza la relación bilateral. Para México es un mercado capital. En 2025 exportó aguacate hacia el norte por valor de 3.600 millones de dólares. Es el segundo producto alimentario más exportado a Estados Unidos. Ese flujo de envíos no ha dejado de crecer en los últimos años al mismo ritmo que el precio y la demanda ocasionada por la revolución gastronómica en torno al llamado oro verde . Y Estados Unidos no puede prescindir de México como proveedor cuando su producción nacional no es suficiente para el consumo interno. El éxito ha hecho que la violencia aparezca en la ecuación. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Trump extiende sus tentáculos militares en Latinoamérica
items.description: Al Gobierno de Donald Trump se le puede acusar de muchas cosas, pero no de ocultar sus verdaderas intenciones en América Latina, que pasan por controlar la región . Esos tentáculos de Estados Unidos en lo que tradicionalmente ha considerado su patio trasero se extienden de diversas formas, desde gobiernos más o menos títeres como la Venezuela de Delcy Rodríguez , a alianzas políticas estrechísimas como la Argentina de Javier Milei pasando por las operaciones militares para imponer sus intereses. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Las siete vidas de Daniela
items.description: Daniela llevaba ya varias horas sepultada cuando alguien, desde una montaña de cascotes , le preguntó su nombre. Ella gritó también el de su hijo. Y después el nombre de su padre. Fue así como los rescatistas supieron que la mujer que acabarían sacando de allí con vida era la misma cuyo rostro y cabello rubio llevaban casi dos días circulando en un cartel: “Se busca. Daniela Andrea Largo Sánchez, 32 años. Desaparecida en Pereira durante el temblor”. Seguir leyendo

items.title: 24-Hour Economy must go beyond slogans – AGI President demands concrete action
items.description: The President of the Association of Ghana Industries (AGI), Seth Twum Akwaboah, has urged government to move beyond slogans and focus on the concrete policies and programmes needed to make Ghana’s 24-Hour Economy work. He said the success of the policy should not be measured by the popularity of its name but by the practical steps taken to change the status quo. “For me, I don’t bother so much about the clichés you create, whether it is 24-Hour Economy or 1D1F; that’s not really the issue for me. It is more of what you do within those policies,” he said on Joy News’ PM Express Business Edition on Thursday. Mr Akwaboah said government must pay particular attention to how policies are developed and implemented. “You can come up with any policy, but then, when you develop the policy, what has gone into the policy development? How consultative was its nature? What are the key policies or activities within the policy that you are trying to implement to change the status quo?” he asked. His comments come as the government continues efforts to operationalise its flagship 24-hour economy policy, which is intended to expand economic activity beyond traditional working hours and create more opportunities for businesses and workers. The AGI President acknowledged that the policy was initially unclear, leading to questions from businesses and other stakeholders. He, however, said consultations with government have helped bring greater clarity to the initiative. “I think we are making good progress because now it’s coming clearer. Government is defining,” he said. Mr Akwaboah cautioned against expectations that the policy would transform the economy overnight. “When you hear a cliché, when you hear a mention of something like that, sometimes the expectation is that overnight things will change and everything will be a 24-hour economy. It doesn’t happen like that,” he explained. He compared the situation to the former government’s One District, One Factory (1D1F) initiative. “The same thing I said is that when we had the 1D1F. All of a sudden, you think that every district is going to have an industry? Government has mentioned it. It’s an intention. It’s a vision. How do we work towards it?” he said. According to him, the focus should now be on identifying the specific interventions needed to make the 24-hour economy a reality. “But then we need to define the specific activities and policies and programs we are going to do to make that happen,” he said. Mr Akwaboah said government has made progress by launching a blueprint for the initiative, which he believes contains ideas capable of transforming economic activity if properly implemented. “And gradually they are coming to that point where now they’ve launched a blueprint, and then in it there are a lot of interesting ideas. If we’re able to implement it to the letter, I’m sure it will help change a lot of things,” he said. He reaffirmed the AGI’s support for the policy and said the association is already engaging the 24-hour economy secretariat on its implementation. “So for me, I embrace it just as we embraced the 1D1F, AGI embraces the 24-hour economy, and we are working with government,” he said. “We are working with the 24-hour economy secretariat to implement some of the things they said they will implement. If we’re able to do it, it will be a game changer,” he added.

items.title: Wildfire destroys homes, forces evacuations near Croatia's Omis
items.description: Strong winds fuel blaze as residents and tourists flee threatened areas

items.title: ¿Por qué internet se ha obsesionado con un libro de más de 500 páginas sobre la sal?
items.description: “Me he leído un libro de 500 páginas sobre la sal y ha arruinado por completo mi capacidad para tener una conversación normal”. Así empezaba un vídeo —ahora viral— que el creador de contenido Wyatt Derman subió hace unas semanas a sus redes sociales contando que no podía parar de hablar sobre este condimento tan cotidiano . “Al principio, eran datos divertidos y relajados: ¿sabías que a los romanos les pagaban en sal?”, explica el joven, que admite que a partir de ahí, no supo parar. “‘Soldado’ viene de sal, ‘ensalada’ viene de sal, ‘salami’, ‘salaz’...”. Deslumbrado por el hecho de que imperios, guerras o protestas tan célebres como la Marcha de la Sal liderada por Gandhi guarden relación con esta sustancia, asegura haberse convertido “en un hombre que no puede pasar el salero sin sentir el peso de la civilización humana”. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Mali says 82 soldiers captured by armed groups have been freed
items.description: Malian army says the soldiers were held prisoner by Tuareg and al-Qaeda-linked armed groups in the northern region.

items.title: Ex-Sindh minister seeks FIR against ex-wife over AI-edited pictures
items.description: KARACHI: Former Sindh minister Ghulam Rasool Unnar has allegedly fallen victim to artificial intelligence (AI) technology, claiming that he discovered after his marriage that pictures of his ex-wife that she had shared with him had been edited and altered using AI. Unnar approa­ched a sessions court seeking registration of an FIR against his ex-wife, Razia Arbab, under the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (PECA) He informed the court that he had come into contact with Ms Arbab through social media platforms. He said that while they were communicating, she proposed marriage to him. According to the applicant, they later got married through a video call in the presence of witnesses, against a dower of Rs100,000, which had already been paid to her. The former minister alleged that during the ceremony, his ex-wife did not reveal her face and kept it covered with a niqab. However, after the marriage, when Mr Unnar met her in person, he “got shocked and surprised” to discover that she had allegedly “cheated and deceived” him by “concealing her real face” and sending filtered and AI-edited pictures before the marriage. He submitted that he subsequently separated from his wife and later divorced her, but she continued posting “fake news” about his death and fabricated images on social media. He further alleged that she was demanding money from him and sending abusive and threatening messages on WhatsApp, warning him that she would share his personal videos or kill him if he did not pay her. Asking the court to order registration of an FIR against her, he stated that by posting fake news and spreading false information, levelling false, shameful and baseless allegations on social media, his ex-wife has committed offences under Peca. He requested the court to direct the concerned SHO to record his statement and register an FIR against his ex-wife. After hearing his submissions, Additional District and Sessions Judge (South) Muhammad Aslam Sheikh issued notices to the SSP Complaint Cell, the SHO of the Defence police station and the proposed accused, directing them to submit their responses before the court on Aug 17. Published in Dawn, August 14th, 2026

items.title: Le dirham s'apprécie de 0,1% face à l'euro entre juin et juillet 2026
items.description: Le dirham s’est apprécié de 0,1% face à l’euro entre les mois de juin et juillet 2026, selon Bank Al-Maghrib (BAM). Face au dollar américain, la monnaie nationale s'est dépréciée de 0,7%, fait savoir la Banque Centrale dans sa récente Revue mensuelle de la conjoncture économique, monétaire et financière, précisant que l’euro s’est déprécié de 0,8% par rapport au dollar américain. En juin 2026, le volume des échanges de devises contre dirham sur le marché interbancaire s’est accru de 13,4% par rapport à l’année précédente, pour s’établir à 32,7 milliards de dirhams (MMDH). Pour ce qui est des opérations entre les banques et leur clientèle, les achats au comptant par la clientèle se sont élevés à 46,8 MMDH en juin, contre 35,3 MMDH un an auparavant, alors que ceux à terme ont totalisé 16,8 MMDH, après 16 MMDH en juin 2025. En parallèle, les ventes se sont chiffrées à 36,5 MMDH, contre 36,3 MMDH, au comptant et à 3 MMDH, après 3,7 MMDH à terme. The post Le dirham s'apprécie de 0,1% face à l'euro entre juin et juillet 2026 appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: ‘Business partner’ granted interim bail in Mir Raza Ali murder case
items.description: KARACHI: A sessions court has granted interim pre-arrest bail to a man said to be a “business partner” of Mir Raza Ali, owner of eatery Wafflix, who had gone missing on July 28 after leaving his home in PECHS, Block-2, and his bullet-riddled body was found a day later. The body was dumped in bushes opposite the University of Karachi near Shahi Qila Ground in Gulistan-i-Jauhar. Muhammad Ahmed Bhardey filed an application before the additional district and sessions judge (East) through his counsel, Khalid Mumtaz, seeking pre-arrest bail in the alleged murder case. After a preliminary hearing, the court granted interim bail to Ahmed against a surety of Rs100,000 and issued notices to the investigating officer and the prosecution for Aug 15, for confirmation or otherwise. Speaking to Dawn , Advocate Mumtaz said the applicant was Raza’s childhood friend and they had been running the business together. He added that Ahmed looked after their branch at Five Star Chowrangi, while Mir Raza managed the Bahadurabad branch. He said Ahmed had approached the court for bail as the police were allegedly harassing him. He added that his client was ready to join the investigation and cooperate with the prosecution. Advocate Mumtaz claimed that Ahmed had already appeared before the police whenever the concerned SHO, SSP or any other official summoned him to record his statement. DSP Lashari to investigate case The investigation team formed by the Sindh IGP and led by DIG Crime & Investigation Amir Farooqi continued its investigation into the kidnapping-cum-murder case of Raza, officials said. DIG Farooqi told Dawn on Thursday that DSP Siraj Lashari had been assigned to investigate the case. He said the team interrogated first responders to the crime scene and also visited the crime scene in detail. Moreover, the team had interviewed the family in detail and recorded their statement. Published in Dawn, August 14th, 2026

items.title: Angry Ekole River: Bayelsa community fights for survival as erosion swallows homes
items.description: By Samuel Oyadongha, Yenagoa Four years ago, Ayi, a resident of Obogoro, a riverside community on the fringe of Yenagoa Local Government Area, Bayelsa State, gathered her six children around her and told them they would have to leave. Not because of conflict, not because of family strife but because the river was coming for their home. “The Ekole River was more than sixteen plots from our house when we moved in, she recalled. “Now that same house is on the verge of being swallowed.” Today, Ayi is a tenant in a neighbouring community, paying rent she can barely afford while her own family home, built with years of sacrifice, teeters on the edge of destruction. She is not alone. A Community Under Siege For years, Obogoro has been a thriving riverside settlement where fishing, farming, and trade sustained families. Civil servants, traders, farmers and strangers lived side by side, their lives intertwined with the ebb and flow of the Ekole River that gave them sustenance. But the river that once gave life is now taking it away. A large portion of the community land has been washed away in the last few years. Coastal erosion has transformed the once vibrant community into a landscape of fear. Homes that stood for decades have crumbled into the water. Farmlands that fed families now lie submerged. Even the community’s Corpers’ Lodge, a symbol of progress and connection to the wider world has been lost to the relentless advance of the wave. The government relocated the community school to safer ground, but for many residents, the damage has already cut too deep. “It’s horrifying staying in my house given the erosion menace,” said Madam Eunice, who fled her home after a terrifying night that will forever haunt her memory. “There was a night when we heard a frightening noise,” she recalled. “When we summoned courage to come out, we discovered that the river had claimed a large portion of land. That was when we realised the risk of staying back.” For four years now, Eunice has been paying “high rent as a tenant” in Yenagoa’s Amarata suburb, even as her own comfortable home stands empty, condemned by the advancing waters. “I have a comfortable home that I was forced to move out of by menacing erosion,” she said, the frustration evident in her voice. Cost Implication The economic toll is devastating. In a region where building materials have become prohibitively expensive, losing a home means losing everything. “Building materials have become very expensive, and nobody wants to lose their property and have to rebuild,” said Egbo Nnamdi, a distressed landlord whose property now stands dangerously close to where a dredger continues to operate. “Even right now, as I’m speaking to you, there is still a dredger operating right in the area, very close to my property,” he added. “We have done everything humanly possible, but we are yet to get relief.” Nnamdi points to unregulated sand mining as a key factor worsening the crisis. Dredgers, he lamented, are operating at the very top of the river, where their activities compound the erosive force of the current. His words, “Those activities are pushing the erosion directly toward the area where they are dredging. If those activities weren’t taking place, the erosion would have already passed that area by now.” A Crisis, Decade in the Making Bayelsa State, with its delicate deltaic geography, has endured decades of coastal erosion, flooding, and land loss. Rising sea levels, tidal surges, and the absence of critical protective infrastructure have left communities like Obogoro and others increasingly vulnerable. Many settlements have lost not just homes, but entire livelihoods. Farmlands have disappeared, access to clean water has been compromised, and families have been forced to scatter inland, fracturing the social fabric that once held communities together. “The situation is very bad,” Nnamdi lamented.. In 2023, the Bayelsa State government intervened, awarding a contract to a local firm to address the crisis. But residents said the situation has only worsened as work stalled. Frank Ovie paints a stark picture of what needs to happen to savage the situation. He said: “What should be done is to divert the river current either by excavating an alternate channel or building a wall at the point where the current is incident on the community. Either way, it will reduce the force of the current.” He urged stakeholders in the community not relent in crying out to the relevant authorities. “They should ensure that the issue continues to dominate public discourse,” he added. Govt Assures The government, on its part, had assured that the erosion control project in the community has not been abandoned. Governor Douye Diri, had years back in a statement by his Chief Press Secretary, Daniel Alabrah, explained that the government was committed to finding a lasting solution to the erosion menace. While empathising with the community over the negative effects of the coastal erosion, including the loss of lives, land, property and sources of livelihood, Diri urged the community to keep faith with the government to rescue the situation. The government, it was further learned, had received a detailed report from the state Ministry of Environment on the Obogoro erosion project and had given directives on how to address the menace permanently. Coastal Erosion, a Major Problem Speaking on the erosion menace confronting the state, Alagoa Morris, Chief Operating Officer, Environmental Conservation, Agriculture and Rural Development (ECARD) and Technical Adviser to the Governor on Environment 1, said besides oil industry induced pollution, coastal and river bank erosion is the the most pervasive environmental and ecological menace faced by communities in the state. Morris listed the communities to include Obogoro, Odi, Northern Kaiama, Anibeze, Sampou, Abobiri, Peremabiri, Olugbobiri, Okpotuwari, Lasukgbene, Odioama, Sangana, Kongho, Twon Brass, Okpoama, Koluama, Foropa, Ekeni, Ezetu, Bilabiri and Amatu among others. Morris, however, described Obogoro as the fastest battered erosion troubled site he had witnessed, making available pictures of the school premises before it was swallowed by the rampaging Ekole River. “We met this school building during our first visit in 2018 or so… next visit in 2019 it became a victim and the community lost it completely to the erosion. Obogoro is the fastest erosion site I have witnessed. See the school building before it was eventually washed away,” ECARD Chief Operating Officer said pointing at the pictures, he once took. A Model Worth Replicating For environmental advocates, the solution lies in aggressive intervention. They point to the Emadike shoreline and land reclamation project in Ogbia Local Government Area carried out by the Federal Government through the Ecological office as a success story worth replicating. “What we have seen at Emadike community is a clear testament that embarking on shoreline protection is quite beneficial to our communities suffering from flooding and coastal erosion,” Morris said. The Emadike project, he noted, has significantly reduced tidal surges and land degradation, offering long-term environmental and economic benefits. “We want to call on the Federal Government and the Ecological Fund Office to replicate the same project in our coastal communities where the locals are constantly threatened by erosion,” Morris noted. A Call to Action Collins Diepreye, a concerned Bayelsan, warned that without urgent government action, more communities along the Ekoli River face total submersion. “Whole communities risk being displaced, leading to heightened socio-economic hardship,” he said. For families like Ayi’s, Madam Eunice’s and others, this is not a mere threat. It is the daily reality of watching your world dissolve into the water. The government has spoken of a redesigned project and plans for permanent solutions. But for residents watching the river inch closer with each passing day, words are not enough. As one resident put it simply: “We are still calling on the government to look into our situation.” For the people of Obogoro, the river that once sustained them now threatens to consume everything they have built. And as the waters continue their advance, they wait not just for intervention, but for hope. The post Angry Ekole River: Bayelsa community fights for survival as erosion swallows homes appeared first on Vanguard News .
